title: Debrief: what could the desk legitimately have known, and is the relationship robust enough to use?
concepts: information set at the decision time
rubric: States what the desk could know at each settlement: the latest weekly report already published (10:30 New York, in UTC, usually 5 days after the week — 12 days once), and monthly demand two months late and in its first-estimate version.

Explains why a database 'as of today' misrepresents the information set: reports attached from the week they describe (929 of 1,510 days use a report not yet published) and revised demand (on average 127 kb/d higher than first seen, 0.67 pp of growth).
Shows how the wrong join created a false relationship (eve-of-release correlation −0.245, t −4.4 vs −0.077 with the correct join) — the release-day reaction relabelled as a forecast.
Separates the reaction (−0.30 % per mb within hours, robust: the information is priced at once) from the drift (t −4.8 with OLS, −2.9 with HAC, concentrated in 2020–2022).

Reports the out-of-sample evidence: on 2023–2024 the frozen model (MAE 6.21 %) and the quarterly walk-forward (6.17 %) are worse than predicting zero (5.98 %); the coefficient shrinks as new data arrive. Conclusion: not robust enough to use.

States the limits of the claims: synthetic, single market; without genuine vintages only pseudo point-in-time is possible; a good out-of-sample result would not have proved causality or future profits.

Ends with a usable recommendation: trade the information at the release (or not at all), stop looking for post-release drift, keep the point-in-time pipeline (availability joins, vintages, truncation tests, purged labels) for any future signal.
